lines.text: I can't see it. Not even close.
The wall is only about six meters wide. From four hundred kilometers, that's like trying to spot a pencil from half a kilometer away.
Then why does everyone say you can?
The claim was already written down in seventeen fifty-four. The first human reached space in nineteen sixty-one.
People repeated it for two hundred years before anyone could check.
So what can you actually see from up here?
This station circles the Earth every ninety minutes. Sixteen sunrises a day. Watch the night side.
Whoa... those lights.
Cities. Most borders are invisible from here. A few are lit up with floodlights, and those you can see.
Up here, a border only shows up if someone switches the lights on.
And that green glow?
An aurora. And those flashes in the clouds are thunderstorms. You're looking down on them.
But the view that really changes people is further out.
In nineteen sixty-eight, three astronauts flew around the Moon to study it. Then the Earth rose over the horizon, and they grabbed a camera.
One of them said they went to explore the Moon, and ended up discovering the Earth.
In nineteen ninety, the Voyager one probe was about six billion kilometers away when it turned its camera back toward home.
Earth was smaller than a single pixel.
Every person you've ever known, every war, every border... all inside that tiny dot.
So what's the change? You said people come back different.
It has a name. The overview effect.
Astronauts describe the same thing. Borders stop mattering. Old arguments feel tiny. And the Earth suddenly looks fragile.
In twenty twenty-one, an actor who played a starship captain for decades finally flew to space, at ninety years old.
Afterwards, he said what he felt most wasn't joy. It was grief.
Grief? Why?
Below him was everything. Above him, nothing but black.
So next time something small ruins your day, remember that dot.
Everything I care about... in one tiny point of light.
